name: Epaphroditus
charge: For the work of Christ he was nigh unto death, not regarding his life, to supply your lack of service toward me
summary: Paul, writing from confinement in Rome, called Epaphroditus his brother, companion in labour, and fellowsoldier, and the congregation’s messenger who ministered to his wants (Philippians 2:25). The brother fell sick near to death carrying that service, and grieved because the congregation had heard of it (Philippians 2:26-27). Paul sent him back with the charge that they receive him with all gladness and hold such in reputation, because for the work of Christ he came near to death, not regarding his life, to supply what their own service to Paul had lacked (Philippians 2:28-30).
offenseFull: Paul could not travel. He was held in Rome, and the work of the congregations had to be carried by men he could trust with letters and with money. Epaphroditus is the man he names, and the titles are stacked: brother, companion in labour, fellowsoldier, your messenger, and he that ministered to my wants (Philippians 2:25). The teaching makes the practical point that Paul had no fear this brother would run off with the collection or edit the doctrine on the road, which is more than can be said for the men calling themselves messengers and pastors now. He is not a famous name. He served a great man and was faithful with the churches’ business. The word fellowsoldier is not ornament either; Paul used it of Archippus too (Philemon 1:2), and it states our actual condition. This is a war. Every man in it is a soldier whatever his rank, told to endure hardness and not to entangle himself with the affairs of this life, so that he may please him who chose him to be a soldier (2 Timothy 2:3-4). Some fall in it, some are taken, some go absent.

He longed after the whole congregation and was full of heaviness because they had heard that he had been sick (Philippians 2:26). Read that again slowly: he was the one lying sick, and his distress was over their distress. Indeed he was sick, near to death, and God had mercy on him, and on Paul also, lest Paul should have sorrow upon sorrow (Philippians 2:27). The Lord does not try a man above what he can bear. Paul was already in chains and downtrodden; taking that brother out of the earth would have been more than the load. And the reason he was in that condition is stated without flattery: for the work of Christ he was near to death, not for his own work and not for a job, and he did not regard his life, to supply what was lacking in their service toward Paul (Philippians 2:30). The Philippians had given before, when no other congregation communicated with him in the matter of giving and receiving, sending to his necessity more than once (Philippians 4:15-16), and Paul called the fresh supply this brother carried an odour of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable and wellpleasing to God (Philippians 4:18).
judgmentFull: Paul sent him back the more carefully, so that they might rejoice at the sight of him and Paul be the less sorrowful, and told them to receive him in the Lord with all gladness and to hold such in reputation (Philippians 2:28-29). That is the blessing pronounced over him, and the teaching insists on what it is worth. A good name is better than precious ointment (Ecclesiastes 7:1). A man is told to have regard to his name, because it continues with him above a thousand great treasures of gold (Ecclesiasticus 41:12). Daniel came out of the matter of Susanna in great reputation in the sight of the people (Susanna 1:64), and when Paul went up to Jerusalem he communicated privately with them which were of reputation (Galatians 2:2). Every brother and sister who comes into this truth is building a name, either as a labourer or as a murmurer and a busybody, and the name follows the man and follows his children after him. Epaphroditus is the pattern of the right kind. He was not famous, which is why the congregation had to be told to honour him. What he was known for was work that almost killed him, done for somebody else’s sake.

Galatians 2: The Council at Jerusalem and Justification by Faith

text.text: Yet I supposed it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my brother, and companion in labour, and fellowsoldier, but your messenger, and he that ministered to my wants.
For he longed after you all, and was full of heaviness, because that ye had heard that he had been sick.
For indeed he was sick nigh unto death: but God had mercy on him; and not on him only, but on me also, lest I should have sorrow upon sorrow.
And to our beloved Apphia, and Archippus our fellowsoldier, and to the church in thy house:
Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ.
No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life; that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a soldier.
I sent him therefore the more carefully, that, when ye see him again, ye may rejoice, and that I may be the less sorrowful.
Receive him therefore in the Lord with all gladness; and hold such in reputation:
Because for the work of Christ he was nigh unto death, not regarding his life, to supply your lack of service toward me.
Now ye Philippians know also, that in the beginning of the gospel, when I departed from Macedonia, no church communicated with me as concerning giving and receiving, but ye only.
For even in Thessalonica ye sent once and again unto my necessity.
Not because I desire a gift: but I desire fruit that may abound to your account.
But I have all, and abound: I am full, having received of Epaphroditus the things which were sent from you, an odour of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable, wellpleasing to God.
A good name is better than precious ointment; and the day of death than the day of one’s birth.
Have regard to thy name; for that shall continue with thee above a thousand great treasures of gold.
From that day forth was Daniel had in great reputation in the sight of the people.

And I went up by revelation, and communicated unto them that gospel which I preach among the Gentiles, but privately to them which were of reputation, lest by any means I should run, or had run, in vain.
